claims.claim: Intelligence is commonly defined as the ability to learn, reason, and solve problems; the APA Dictionary of Psychology defines intelligence as the ability to derive information, learn from experience, adapt to the environment, understand, and correctly utilize thought and reason, and the Noba Project describes intellectual ability as encompassing the ability to learn, remember, and use new information, to solve problems, and to adapt to novel situations.

Experts continue to debate the definition of intelligence; OpenStax Psychology 2e notes that the way researchers have defined the concept of intelligence has been modified many times since the birth of psychology, and the Noba Project calls intelligence one of the oldest and longest-studied topics in psychology.

IQ stands for intelligence quotient and describes a standard score earned on a test designed to measure intelligence; the average is customarily set at 100, with slightly more than two thirds of scores falling within plus or minus 15 points of the mean.
Alfred Binet was asked by the French government to develop an intelligence test to use on children, to determine which ones might have difficulty in school so they could get help.

Louis Terman, a Stanford professor, standardized Binet's work into the Stanford-Binet Intelligence Scale, and David Wechsler developed the Wechsler scales (starting 1939) from subtests covering verbal and nonverbal skills, believing intelligence to be a global capacity to act purposefully, think rationally, and deal effectively with the environment.

Charles Spearman proposed that intelligence consists of one general factor, g, which could be measured and compared among individuals; the APA Dictionary credits the general factor (symbol: g) as postulated in 1904 by Charles Spearman and as a basic ability underlying performance of different varieties of intellectual tasks.

Howard Gardner's theory of multiple intelligences holds that each person possesses at least eight relatively independent intelligences (linguistic, logical-mathematical, musical, bodily-kinesthetic, spatial, interpersonal, intrapersonal, and naturalistic); OpenStax reports the theory is widely used in education but has been heavily criticized among cognitive psychologists for lacking empirical evidence.
Robert Sternberg's triarchic theory of intelligence proposes three key abilities — analytical, creative, and practical — viewed as largely (although not entirely) distinct.

Modern intelligence tests measure abilities such as solving problems, forming concepts, reasoning, and acquiring detail, but they do not capture the whole person: IQ tests have been the subject of debate throughout their development and use (including harmful uses such as supporting the eugenics movement), David Wechsler was suspicious of using a single score to capture all of intelligence, and the question of how valid intelligence tests are remains open.

Scores on intelligence tests have risen across generations (the Flynn effect, named after James Flynn), and Flynn argued that increased IQ scores do not necessarily mean younger generations are more intelligent.

Genes and environment both shape intelligence: in the Minnesota Study of Twins Reared Apart, identical twins raised together and identical twins raised apart showed higher correlations between their IQ scores than siblings or fraternal twins raised together, revealing a genetic component; OpenStax concludes that aspects of each idea are probably correct, and the range-of-reaction view holds that a person's genetic potential is a fixed quantity while reaching it depends on environmental stimulation, especially in childhood.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is intelligence one general ability or many distinct abilities?
positions: Spearman's g: a single general factor underlies performance across many kinds of intellectual tasks
Gardner's multiple intelligences: at least eight relatively independent intelligences
Sternberg's triarchic theory: three largely distinct abilities (analytical, creative, practical)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents each theory with attribution to its originator, notes that Gardner's theory is widely used in education but heavily criticized among cognitive psychologists for lacking empirical evidence, and frames the one-versus-many question as an open scientific debate rather than a settled fact.

positions: APA Dictionary: the ability to derive information, learn from experience, adapt to the environment, understand, and correctly utilize thought and reason
Noba Project and OpenStax: emphasis on learning, problem solving, and adapting to novel situations
Some researchers argue for a single broad ability; others for a collection of distinct abilities
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson adopts a working definition — the ability to learn, reason, and solve problems — presented as a synthesis, explicitly attributed to the APA Dictionary and Noba Project, with the honest note that experts continue to debate the definition.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Nature versus nurture: what shapes intelligence?
positions: Genetic inheritance: twin-study correlations show a genetic component
Developmental environment: stimulation and experience shape intellectual development
Range of reaction: genetic potential is fixed, but reaching it depends on environmental stimulation
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both contribute. The lesson states each position with attribution, uses no invented statistics, and presents the conclusion in OpenStax's own words: the reality is that aspects of each idea are probably correct.

sourceRecords.title: IQ — APA Dictionary of Psychology
sourceRecords.notes: Read via the dictionary's public definitions API (getdopdefinitions?q=iq) on 2026-08-22. Entry: intelligence quotient as a standard measure of an individual's intelligence level based on psychological tests; mean customarily 100; slightly more than two thirds of scores within plus or minus 15 points (one standard deviation); early ratio IQ (mental age / chronological age x 100) mostly replaced by deviation IQ. Supports the IQ explanation. Paraphrased only.

sourceRecords.title: Intelligence test — APA Dictionary of Psychology
sourceRecords.notes: Read via the dictionary's public definitions API (getdopdefinitions?q=intelligence-test) on 2026-08-22. Entry: an individually administered test used to determine a person's level of intelligence by measuring their ability to solve problems, form concepts, reason, acquire detail, and perform other intellectual tasks; examples include the Stanford-Binet Intelligence Scale and the Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale. Supports the 'tests today' section. Paraphrased only.

sourceRecords.title: General factor — APA Dictionary of Psychology
sourceRecords.notes: Read via the dictionary's public definitions API (getdopdefinitions?q=general-factor) on 2026-08-22. Entry: the general factor (symbol: g), a hypothetical source of individual differences in general ability, a basic ability underlying the performance of different varieties of intellectual tasks; postulated in 1904 by Charles Spearman. Supports the Spearman g claim with attribution. Paraphrased only.

sourceRecords.title: Triarchic theory of intelligence — APA Dictionary of Psychology
sourceRecords.notes: Read via the dictionary's public definitions API (getdopdefinitions?q=triarchic-theory-of-intelligence) on 2026-08-22. Entry: a theory of intelligence in which three key abilities — analytical, creative, and practical — are viewed as largely (although not entirely) distinct; proposed in 1985 by Robert J. Sternberg. Supports the Sternberg triarchic claim with attribution. Paraphrased only.

sourceRecords.title: Heritability — APA Dictionary of Psychology
